extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, data-center operators, and public-health professionals concerned with environmental and health impacts of computing
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and methodological research that quantifies lifecycle pollutant emissions from data centers and their public-health impacts, and develops operational/ reporting recommendations to mitigate those impacts. Includes modeling, projection, distributional equity analysis, and scheduling-framework designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model lifecycle pollutant emissions for data centers and computing tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduces a principled methodology to model lifecycle pollutant emissions for data centers and computing tasks, covering the lifecycle from chip manufacturing to operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly account for emissions of criteria air pollutants such as fine particulate matter (PM2.5) across the full lifecycle (manufacturing through operation) when estimating impacts. The paper's methodology is posed as a template for quantifying pollutant emissions attributable to specific computing tasks (e.g., training large AI models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify public health impacts and monetize health burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify the public health impacts of lifecycle emissions and express the burden in monetary terms (e.g., projecting total annual public health burden of U.S. data centers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the emissions model output to estimate health outcomes and convert those to monetary public-health cost estimates for comparison with other sources (the paper projects >$20 billion annual burden in 2028). Update projections using best-available reports and simulation results (e.g., LBNL report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess distributional impacts across communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how public health costs are distributed across different communities and identify disproportionate burdens borne by disadvantaged communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report per-household health burden and distributional disparities (the paper finds per-household burdens up to 200x higher in more-impacted communities). Policymaking and mitigation should prioritize attention to all impacted and disadvantaged communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate public-health risk as an operational scheduling metric (health-informed computing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a health-informed computing framework that explicitly incorporates public-health risk as a key metric for scheduling data-center workloads across space and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design workload scheduling policies that optimize not only traditional metrics (e.g., latency, cost, carbon) but also minimize public-health risks from pollutant emissions; simulations in the paper show such scheduling can effectively mitigate adverse health impacts while advancing environmental sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a standard reporting protocol for public-health impacts of data centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend adopting a standard reporting protocol for the public-health impacts of data centers and ensuring transparent reporting of impacts on all communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish standardized metrics and disclosure practices so stakeholders can compare and audit public-health impacts across operators and regions. Reporting should include lifecycle emissions, monetized health burdens, distributional effects, and the assumptions/methods used for projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative framing/benchmarks to communicate impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame and communicate computed impacts using relatable benchmarks (e.g., comparing emissions from training a large AI model to >10,000 round trips by car between Los Angeles and New York City).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide contextual comparisons to familiar sources of pollution to make health-impact estimates understandable to policymakers and the public; use such comparisons to motivate mitigation and policy responses.
